overview:
The rupture came fast. In 1945 the United States and the Soviet Union had just finished winning a war together; within two years they were organizing the world against each other. The occupation of Germany hardened into partition, Soviet-backed governments consolidated across Eastern Europe, and in March 1947 Truman asked Congress for aid to Greece and Turkey with an argument that quietly committed the United States to supporting "free peoples" anywhere — a break from the older American habit of staying out of distant quarrels. The Marshall Plan followed, then the Berlin Blockade of 1948–49, when Stalin cut the western sectors of the city off from land access and the Allies supplied two million people by air for eleven months. NATO was founded in 1949; the Soviets tested an atomic bomb the same year, and Communists won the Chinese civil war. By 1950, with the annexation of Tibet and the outbreak of war in Korea, the confrontation had gone global and had acquired the feature that defined it: two arsenals large enough that neither side could risk a direct fight.

So the fighting happened elsewhere, and by proxy. The events gathered here trace that displacement outward — a British destroyer mined in Albanian waters in 1946, workers shot down in Poznań in 1956, Berlin split by a wall in 1961, Soviet missiles found in Cuba in October 1962 in the crisis that came closest to nuclear war, Egyptian and Israeli forces grinding at each other across the Suez Canal in 1969 with Soviet crews manning air defenses, civil wars in Guatemala and Ethiopia that outlasted the superpower interest that fed them. Détente in the 1970s produced arms-control treaties without ending any of this, and collapsed after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979. Even the low-grade naval and air brushes — American and Soviet ships bumping hulls in the Black Sea in 1986, American fighters downing Libyan jets over the Gulf of Sidra in 1989 — were the same contest at a smaller scale.

The ending was not symmetrical. Mikhail Gorbachev's attempts to reform the Soviet system from 1985 loosened Moscow's grip on Eastern Europe, and in 1989 the Communist governments there fell in months, mostly without bloodshed; the Berlin Wall opened in November. That same year, in Beijing, the Chinese leadership answered its own protest movement with troops and tanks in Tiananmen Square, and the Communist Party survived — a reminder that 1989 did not mean the same thing everywhere. The Soviet Union itself dissolved at the end of 1991. The best estimates put something like twenty million dead in the wars of these decades, and almost none of them died in Europe, where the confrontation began.
significance: Almost every feature of the contemporary international order was set in these decades: the borders of divided states, the alliance systems, the nuclear arsenals and the arms-control machinery built to manage them, the international financial institutions, the shape of decolonization as it was funneled through superpower patronage. The Cold War also determined which postcolonial states got weapons and which got aid, and installed or propped up governments whose consequences long outlived the reason they were installed — Guatemala's civil war ran to 1996, Afghanistan's fighting never really stopped. Its end left the United States briefly without a peer and left a generation of scholars, newly admitted to Soviet and Chinese archives, rewriting what everyone had thought they knew.
coverage: Written from the standard reference accounts plus the U.S. State Department's own history of containment and the Wilson Center's Cold War International History Project, which exists precisely because the field was built for forty years on Western documents alone; Soviet, Chinese, and Eastern European records opened only after 1991 and remain unevenly accessible, with Russian archives having largely reclosed since. The eighteen events in this dataset are heavily weighted toward Europe, superpower crises, and naval incidents, and thin on Asia, Latin America, and Africa, where nearly all the actual killing happened — Korea, Vietnam, Angola, and Afghanistan are absent here, and the human cost figures cited by historians are estimates with wide margins.
